Photograph: Kenya Red Cross Handout/EPA Kenya Five Americans among seven killed in safari helicopter crash in Kenya Officials say all seven people onboard killed, including Telemundo executive and Ecuador intelligence chief Associated Press Wed 19 Aug 2026 16.17 EDT Last modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 16.33 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Seven people, including five Americans, were killed when a safari helicopter crashed on Wednesday morning in a remote part of northern Kenya , according to local police and the state department. Among the dead were an executive with Telemundo, the US-based Spanish-language network owned by NBC Universal, and the director of Ecuador’s national intelligence service. The helicopter crashed at 9.13am while flying from the Loisaba Conservancy to the Ewaso Nyiro area in Samburu county, according to the Kenya Civil Aviation Authority, which said in a statement that an investigation was under way. It said there were seven people onboard – six passengers and the pilot. Late on Wednesday, David Nkoroi, the police commander for Samburu, told reporters that all seven people onboard had died. In Washington, the state department said five of those killed were US citizens. “The US embassy is in touch with local authorities and is providing consular assistance,” it said. “We extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones on their loss.” The identities of the victims were not revealed but a local television station in Miami, Florida, said that José Suárez, 55, president and GM of several Telemundo stations in Florida, was among those killed. “We are heartbroken to learn the tragic news that José was killed in a helicopter accident in Kenya,” the NBC affiliate in Miami quoted from a joint statement from NBC Universal and Telemundo leadership. The helicopter crashed in a rugged area in the foothills of Mount Ololokwe, a popular tourist destination in the country, local media reported. The helicopter, owned by local company Lady Lori Helicopters, was carrying guests with the travel company +Beyond. Lady Lori Helicopters said in a statement that the aircraft was operating a charter flight when it crashed. Tropic Air Kenya, a local safari operator, said in a statement that it dispatched two of its helicopters to aid search and rescue operations. The aviation authority said the aircraft was a Eurocopter EC130 B4. Ecuador confirmed later on Wednesday that Michele Sensi-Contugi, director of the country’s national intelligence center, died in the helicopter crash in Kenya. In a statement posted on X, the presidency said: “In this moment of deep sorrow, the government extends its heartfelt condolences to his family, loved ones and close associates.” Sensi-Contugi was visiting Kenya as a tourist with his wife, Stephany Hollihan Vasconez, who also died in the crash. She was a US and Ecuadorian citizen. They are survived by their two children. Helicopter crashes have happened with increasing regularity in Kenya, which has a thriving tourism industry that depends on domestic carriers to ferry visitors to distant places like Mount Ololokwe. In February, a legislator was among six people who died after a helicopter crash in a hilly area of western Kenya. https://www.digi24.ro/stiri/externe/rusi.text: Deficitul de carburanţi a reapărut în cel puţin şase regiuni ale Rusiei, după ce Ucraina a atacat cel puţin opt rafinării importante în ultimele două săptămâni. Autorităţile au introdus restricţii la vânzarea benzinei şi motorinei, în încercarea de a preveni cumpărăturile de panică şi formarea cozilor la benzinării, transmite Reuters. Ucraina şi-a intensificat atacurile asupra infrastructurii petroliere ruseşti după 30 octombrie, când armistiţiul energetic anunţat de preşedintele american Donald Trump între Moscova şi Kiev nu a intrat efectiv în vigoare. Cel mai recent atac a vizat rafinăria din Kirishi, a doua ca mărime din Rusia, potrivit guvernatorului regiunii Leningrad, Alexander Drozdenko. În regiunea Karelia, autorităţile au limitat alimentarea la 30 de litri de benzină şi 50 de litri de motorină pentru fiecare achiziţie, la staţiile Rosneft de pe principalele şosele. Vânzarea carburanţilor în canistre a fost suspendată complet. „Sunt pe deplin conştient că aceste restricţii pot provoca neplăceri locuitorilor şi companiilor ale căror activităţi depind de transport. Totuşi, în circumstanţele actuale, aceste măsuri sunt necesare”, a declarat guvernatorul regiunii Karelia, Artur Parfenchikov, notează News.ro. Acesta a explicat că prioritatea autorităţilor este prevenirea achiziţiilor de panică, distribuirea uniformă a carburanţilor şi menţinerea funcţionării benzinăriilor. Restricţiile sunt prezentate drept temporare, iar autorităţile încearcă să restabilească aprovizionarea normală. Măsuri similare au fost introduse în Buriatia, în estul Siberiei, inclusiv în capitala regională Ulan-Ude, precum şi în regiunea învecinată Zabaikalsk. Restricţii au fost raportate şi în regiunile Nijni Novgorod, Arhanghelsk, Penza şi Krasnoiarsk. Atacurile ucrainene reduc capacitatea Rusiei de a produce benzină şi motorină, afectând aprovizionarea pieţei interne şi complicând potenţial acordul dintre Vladimir Putin şi Donald Trump privind exporturile ruseşti de motorină către pieţele internaţionale şi Statele Unite. Rusia s-a confruntat cu o criză similară în timpul verii, când atacurile ucrainene cu drone asupra rafinăriilor au coincis cu vârful sezonier al cererii. Moscova a reintrodus atunci restricţii asupra exporturilor de benzină, iar în iulie a limitat şi vânzările externe de motorină. Urmărește știrile Digi24.ro și pe Google News

https://www.delfi.lt/en/politics/could-p.text: Delfi EN Delfi Politics 2026.10.29 06:00 Could Putin attack Europe? The element of madness could have devastating consequences Greta Klimkaitė Source: Delfi EN Vladimir Putin PHOTO: Alexander Kazakov | AP / Scanpix Follow Delfi on Google Rockets and drones entering NATO territory are fuelling tensions in Europe. Leaders of countries and intelligence agencies have spoken about the threat from Russia, and the United States has also issued warnings. Some analysts say the Kremlin could be ready for military action within just a few years. Is that likely? Former Chief of Defence Jonas Vytautas Žukas believes the situation has not yet reached the point where Russia is deliberately attacking the Baltic states. He points out that, otherwise, NATO would already be discussing what steps to take. "We need to look, observe and draw conclusions. None of the investigations carried out so far supports that view. If it is confirmed, we will have a new and very specific situation – a military situation directed against the Baltic states or other frontline countries. Then we will need to talk within NATO: what do we do? Do we activate Article 5? What are our next steps, and what are our defence plans? That would amount to a declaration of war, a direct attack on one country or another. If it is established that a group of drones has been launched, or that they have been deliberately directed at NATO countries, we will be facing a new situation. In that situation, we will have to sit down and consider what to do next and what our political will is: to respond, ignore it or act in some other way," the general says. Former Defence Minister Dovilė Šakalienė also says it is not currently possible to establish that Russia is acting with direct intent. However, she points to a change over the past year. The politician notes that until the summer of 2025, only unarmed objects had entered Lithuania, whereas since July last year NATO countries have been detecting rockets and drones carrying explosives on their territory. "So what are we seeing now? Legally, I might even call it indirect intent: although we are not the direct target, the aggressor understands the potential harm that could result. Even so, it fully accepts that there may be consequences on NATO territory," D. Šakalienė says. The number of drones flying near our territory has risen rapidly in recent years, increasing the likelihood that some of them will enter Lithuanian airspace. D. Šakalienė also notes that electronic warfare capabilities are advancing. "Given this situation, we need to be better prepared for a more intense pattern of airspace violations, even though we do not see direct intent. < ...> The equipment we have acquired – air defence systems bought while I was still minister, both weapons and sensors – is critically important. If you cannot see it, what are you going to shoot at, and what are you going to defend against? Additional active and passive radars have been ordered; a decision taken during my time in office on an acoustic system is finally being implemented; and decisions have also been made to acquire Ukrainian interceptor drones. So I would say we are rapidly adding to our toolkit," the former minister says, listing the measures. NATO air defence is currently in a transitional phase, D. Šakalienė says. "We are beginning to see that we need far more capacity in quantitative terms, because we have to cover much more airspace, and cover it much more densely," she says. J. V. Žukas stresses that drones entering our airspace are also a way of stirring up anxiety. "There is an element of intimidation here. Of course, a drone or two could be deliberately directed at the Baltic states simply to test the response and keep this anxiety going. After that drone flew through, people were again talking about air defence capabilities, even though all countries have similar problems – Poland, Romania and Moldova included. Look at what is happening in Romania: an alert is issued there every day. These problems affect everyone, but the aim is to keep people tense and anxious, simply to say: ’There you are – you launched one by accident.’ We are living in peacetime. We have not deployed our air defence capabilities along the border or near important strategic sites in the way we would in wartime. They want to exploit that now. They want to keep society in this state of tension, while also trying to discredit NATO, make fun of it and see how it responds," J. V. Žukas says. The former chief of defence says such incidents are intended to keep people frightened. So far, the response from European countries has been inadequate. "Only now, at the last minute, have people begun to realise that the danger could be very real. After a drone appeared in Leipzig, after air traffic was disrupted at airports in Denmark and elsewhere… Only now have the politicians responsible started thinking about what to do and what might happen next. We have also seen various expert assessments saying that major events may be approaching and that we need to make exceptional preparations, particularly on Poland’s part. There has been a response, but no decisions. So far, there has been no political will to take joint, very specific action – perhaps to move out of a peacetime posture, raise our combat readiness or shift to some higher level," the general says. Šakalienė: Russia and China are preparing for military action D. Šakalienė identifies 2027–2029 as a critical period. She points out that, despite its losses in Ukraine, Russia continues to develop its military industry, carry out military reform and receive economic support from China. "The processes unfolding in Russia, China, North Korea and Iran are increasingly converging into a single entity. Even if some of their actions may not appear to be directly coordinated at the moment, when you look at their targets, their methods and the regions in which they operate, a very clear, shared systemic picture emerges. For example, Iran is currently depleting certain US weapons systems very effectively – systems that would be critically important in a large-scale conflict. China buys 90 per cent of Iran’s crude oil. Russia has signed a contract worth half a billion dollars with Iran, is selling it MANPADS systems and has put Iranian satellites into orbit. These help monitor territory and improve targeting of the same US base locations. We can see China training Russian soldiers who fought in Ukraine or, after returning to their units in Russia, are training other Russian soldiers," the former minister says. She also says that China’s military will be fully ready for an invasion in the Indo-Pacific region in 2027. She stresses that Taiwan is not the only place at risk: colleagues and experts in Australia, South Korea, Japan and the Philippines describe Beijing’s behaviour as unusually aggressive. "Against this whole backdrop, the Chinese will be ready. Russia is moving forward despite its losses. Another wave of mobilisation is planned and could take place. If, by some political misstep, sanctions on Russia were eased, for example, that would give it additional opportunities to organise some kind of kinetic attack, even on a limited scale. Iran and the Middle East are ablaze. American weapons are being burned through. Russia continues to advance, and China continues its preparations," D. Šakalienė says. She has no doubt that China and Russia will coordinate their actions. "It is clear that Xi Jinping will call Putin when he is ready to begin an invasion in the Indo-Pacific region, so that Putin can ensure Europe has problems of its own and is kept busy. In this situation, 2027–2029 will still be a period of growth for us: our defence industry, our defence capabilities and our ability to hit precise targets are all still developing. This is a bad period. A lot of things here are planned through to 2030, but we cannot wait until 2030. Five per cent – how many countries in this region are there? Four? But all of NATO needs to spend five per cent if we are to develop all those capabilities now. I think anyone who gives the map and international news a glance can see this," the politician warns. Žukas sceptical about claims that Russia could attack in two or three years The former chief of defence is more sceptical about such assessments. He says the mood in the Russian press and among so-called "Z-bloggers" is rather bleak over the war in Ukraine, with a degree of opposition to the Kremlin and Vladimir Putin himself emerging. In addition, Putin is being given a more favourable assessment of the situation than is warranted. The Russians have lost the initiative on the front line, are facing serious personnel problems, and possible mobilisation "does not bode well for them either", J. V. Žukas believes. "In any case, I know the Russian military to some extent. I observe it from the inside – what they say and what they comment on. Morale is very bad, very depressed. Talk of them opening a front or carrying out some kind of invasion in two or three years seems unfounded to me. I am sceptical about that," he says. The general points out that there are no forces left in Kaliningrad either. "As an example, take the 11th Army Corps based in the Kaliningrad region, which consisted of 20,000 people. The entire corps is in Ukraine, in the Kharkiv region. There is nothing in the Kaliningrad region at the moment. The corps has suffered enormous losses. It was defeated during Ukraine’s counter-offensive in 2022 and has been restructured several times. The average age of its soldiers is 40 to 50. It has been filled with poor-quality recruits from among prisoners and various social and anti-social groups, and so on. It has enormous problems," J. V. Žukas says. Dissatisfaction with V. Putin is also growing. "When you read their comments and some of their public statements, I do not think everything is going so well for Russia that it could prepare for a war and be stronger in three years than it was in 2022, when thousands of junior and senior officers were killed, so much equipment was destroyed and the country was already facing such serious economic problems. It would not take much for some kind of tectonic shift or very serious new developments to begin inside Russia itself," the general says. Even if V. Putin decided to launch a limited kinetic attack, he would achieve nothing by doing so, J. V. Žukas says. He also doubts that Russia’s military reform or mobilisation will succeed. What is happening now may amount to spontaneous actions intended to frighten the West and keep society on edge. V. Putin and his inner circle see the end of the war in Ukraine as an existential threat. The former chief of defence hopes that some forces will emerge inside Russia that recognise how hopeless the situation is. The first signs are already appearing, the general says. "When the military conflict ends, there will be another huge danger. There is enormous dissatisfaction within the Russian military. People are exhausted, exploited and shot at; corruption is rampant, drug addiction is widespread – it is hell. People there are also at breaking point and understand how pointless their actions are. These are the kinds of things Putin himself is very afraid of. It is impossible to know how all this might unfold within Russia. That element of madness – when Putin realises that stopping the fighting could mean his physical destruction – could lead to unforeseeable consequences. That is the great risk. If he, his inner circle and the propagandists, who know that their existence is physically coming to an end, are finished, it could have very serious consequences for all of us. But I believe there are people, including within the Russian president’s circle, who understand the situation rationally. There are signs of a split, and of more moderate people who want to end the conflict. That could happen within Putin’s own circle," J. V. Žukas says.
